President Kagame engages with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during a break of the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia, as Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe looks on

For much of Monday morning, November 16, Rwanda was waiting.

Across the country, people followed developments in Cambodia through their smartphones, television screens, radio stations and social media, hoping for news about the future of Louise Mushikiwabo, the Rwandan who has led the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) since 2018.

The negotiations in Phnom Penh were far more complicated than the question many Rwandans were following.

Behind closed doors, leaders were engaged in intense diplomatic manoeuvres, competing proposals and last-minute efforts to prevent a confrontation that threatened to split the organisation.

The drama included reports that Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi left the final meeting before the official announcement, while his Foreign Minister, Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, was captured on camera appearing visibly distressed and confronting a camera operator.

The scenes offered a glimpse of the tension surrounding a contest that had become deeply entangled in the Rwanda-DRC political rivalry.

The eventual decision was to postpone the election of a new Secretary-General for one year, allowing Mushikiwabo to remain in office during the transition. She will not seek another term, and Rwanda has committed not to present a candidate in the next contest.

The compromise, largely credited to Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, prevented an immediate rupture but ended Rwanda’s bid to secure a third consecutive term for Mushikiwabo.

The election had become much more than a contest between four candidates. It was increasingly a reflection of the deteriorating relationship between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Kinshasa strongly opposed Mushikiwabo’s third-term bid and threatened to leave the OIF if she was re-elected. It nominated Juliana Amato Lumumba, daughter of Congo’s independence leader Patrice Lumumba, to challenge the Rwandan incumbent.

The other candidates were Mauritania’s Coumba Bâ and Romania’s former Prime Minister Dacian Cioloș.

Lumumba’s candidacy, however, was itself surrounded by controversy. Reports circulating before the summit suggested that she was unhappy with the level of support she had received from her own government. She was reportedly frustrated that promises of diplomatic lobbying and financial backing had not materialised, leaving her struggling to build support among member states.

The claims raised questions about whether Kinshasa had mounted a serious campaign for its candidate or was primarily using her nomination to challenge Rwanda’s bid. Some Congolese commentators subsequently portrayed her withdrawal as an abandonment of a candidate who had not received the support she expected. These accounts have not been independently established, but they added another layer to the political drama.

Macron’s intervention and Rwanda’s resistance

France also became deeply involved in efforts to prevent the leadership dispute from dividing the organisation.

President Emmanuel Macron reportedly asked President Paul Kagame to consider withdrawing Mushikiwabo’s candidacy to make way for a consensus candidate. Cioloș was among the names discussed.

Rwanda rejected the pressure. Foreign Affairs Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe argued that no country could dictate which candidate another member state should present.

DRC, meanwhile, indicated that it was prepared to withdraw Lumumba’s candidacy and consider supporting Cioloș as part of efforts to reach consensus. The precise status of that withdrawal before the final decision was not entirely clear.

The disagreement exposed the influence of France, the OIF’s largest financial contributor, and revived questions about whether its former colonial power should play such a decisive role in the organisation’s leadership process.

As negotiations dragged on, Senegal’s Faye emerged as a central figure in the search for a solution.

He initiated consultations among leaders and pushed a formula that allowed the different sides to avoid a direct confrontation over the election.

Under the compromise, Mushikiwabo will remain in office for another 12 months. Rwanda will not field a candidate in the next election, while existing candidacies remain open and new candidates may be presented. The organisation will also review the rules governing the selection of its Secretary-General.

The arrangement gave both Kigali and Kinshasa something to take home. Rwanda retained Mushikiwabo in office for another year, while DRC secured an outcome that prevents her from seeking an immediate third term.

Kayikwamba Wagner later welcomed what she called a “wise compromise”, saying it would preserve the unity of the Francophonie. France also welcomed the agreement. Cioloș, however, described the postponement as “a very sad day” for the organisation.

The intensity of the reaction in Rwanda reflected how closely the contest had become associated with the country’s international profile.

For many Rwandans, Mushikiwabo’s position was not simply an appointment within an international organisation. Her eight years at the helm had made the OIF more visible in the country’s public conversation. One Ugandan social media user observed that they had only become aware of the Francophonie after Mushikiwabo became its Secretary-General. The comment was an individual reaction, but it illustrated the visibility her leadership had brought to the organisation.

The outcome was not the clear victory some Rwandans had hoped for. Mushikiwabo remains in office, but the prospect of another Rwandan term has been removed from the next election.

The postponement is also unprecedented in the history of the Secretary-General’s office, created in 1997. Previous leaders were selected through consensus, but the Phnom Penh summit showed how difficult that approach has become amid growing political divisions.

The OIF was already weakened by the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso. Losing DRC, which has the world’s largest French-speaking population, would have dealt another serious blow to its influence.

Phnom Penh avoided an immediate split. But the extraordinary scenes, diplomatic pressure and competing national interests surrounding the election exposed an organisation whose unity is increasingly difficult to preserve.

Gérard Depardieu appeared at a courthouse in Paris on Monday for his appeal trial that was due to start

French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault , admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.

On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.

"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.

It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.

"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court.

"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.

In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.

"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.

"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.

"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."

The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.

Depardieu's lawyers David-Olivier Kaminski (L) and Delphine Meillet (R) were at the courthouse on Monday for the opening day of their client's appeal trial in Paris

His new lawyers, Delphine Meillet and David-Olivier Kaminski, said that with his admission of guilt Depardieu wanted to "move on", adding that "basically, as he turns 78 years old, he is saying to himself that life is more beautiful than 10 days of court hearings".

In the original trial, Depardieu was said to have touched the two women on intimate parts of the body during the making of Les Volets Verts, which is a film about an ageing actor coming to terms with his declining powers.

He himself admitted to using vulgar language but denied being "a metro-train groper". However, he also said he did not consider touching a woman's buttocks to be an act of "sexual aggression".

The trial was the first time the star of films like Green Card and Cyrano de Bergerac appeared in court on sexual assault charges. Several other women have made similar allegations in the media.

A decision on whether an alleged rape case can come to trial is expected this month.

Former Liverpool full-back Neco Williams has 67 Wales caps, scoring five goals

Wales will be without right-back Neco Williams for their final Nations League group match against reigning champions Portugal on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), while goalkeeper Karl Darlow is a doubt.

Nottingham Forest's Williams has been ruled out after he was injured during Saturday's 3-1 defeat in Norway, while Manchester United's Darlow missed training on Monday and will be assessed further.

Midfielder Ethan Ampadu will also miss out at Cardiff City Stadium because of suspension, but centre-back Ben Cabango and winger Sorba Thomas are available after serving one-match bans.

Wales will finish bottom of Group A4 whatever happens against leaders Portugal, and Craig Bellamy's side will have a relegation play-off in March against one of the League B runners-up for a place in the top tier.

"One or two players had to come off through injury [in Norway]. One or two have come through; one or two haven't," said Bellamy.

"Neco's going to be out. Darlow, we'll wait and see later, and everyone else is fully fit."

What Wales need to stay in Nations League top tier

With less riding on this fixture than there might have been, Bellamy could be tempted to make further changes to his side from the loss in Oslo.

Cardiff City attacking midfielder Rubin Colwill shone as a substitute, while Bournemouth's David Brooks came off the bench to score an excellent goal.

Colwill's performance was a particularly popular talking point among fans, many of whom have long been calling for the 24-year-old playmaker to feature more regularly for Wales.

"Rubin's been pushing [to start] for a while," said Bellamy. "Once you get this kid in the final third, then he's a player. We've just got to get him in those areas.

"But he's also got to offer us without the ball as well. If you're not good without the ball, you cannot be a top player.

"If you want a lesson tomorrow without the ball, watch Vitinha [Portugal's Paris St-Germain midfielder] if he plays.

"Rubin has moved [up a level] and long may that continue, because if it does Wales have got a brilliant player.

"I'm more harsh on Rubin because I've known him since he was so young, but credit to him and his manager at Cardiff [Brian Barry-Murphy].

"He's helping develop a real player for us that's going to hopefully have a huge impact for the next five to 10 years."

Etzebeth returns to a starting line-up that boasts 934 Test caps

South Africa record cap holder Eben Etzebeth has been recalled for Saturday's much-anticipated Nations Championship game against Ireland in Dublin.

Etzebeth, 35, missed the Springboks' win over Italy and defeat by France because of injury, but replaces Lood de Jager to earn a record-extending 148th Test cap alongside Ruan Nortje in the world champions' second row.

Cameron Hanekom is named at number eight, replacing Jasper Wiese, who is facing a possible ban after being sent off for a dangerous clear-out in the France game .

Hanekom joins captain Siya Kolisi and two-time World Rugby player of the year Pieter-Steph du Toit in the back row, with Marco van Staden replacing Hanekom on the bench.

Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw are named as the starting front row at the Aviva Stadium (16:40 GMT).

Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus also named Nche, Marx and Louw to start the France game but swapped them out for Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit shortly before kick-off at the Stade de France.

"This is a massive match for us and we know the magnitude of facing Ireland in Dublin, so we felt it was important to strike a balance between consistency in selection, while managing some players and giving others who have been training hard and putting up their hands a chance," said Erasmus.

"Eben has been training well since joining us last week and his leadership, experience and knowledge of playing in vital games will be good for us this week, while we know what physicality and skill Cameron brings, and the same applies to Ox, Malcolm, and Wilco."

Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast is the first player to be cited over a hip drop tackle

Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast is in danger of missing Saturday's Nations Championship match against South Africa after being cited for a tackle against Fiji.

Prendergast will face a disciplinary process for a hip-drop tackle on Fijian captain Peceli Yato in the first half of Ireland's 43-15 win in Dublin on Saturday.

The technique, when a tackling player drops their hips and bodyweight on to the ball-carrier's legs, was outlawed by World Rugby before November's internationals and the 23-year-old is the first player to be cited over its use in a game.

If found guilty and he accepts the verdict, Prendergast could face a pre-determined sanction through the Six Nations' expedited disciplinary process.

However, if he does not accept the charge then he would be referred to a panel to determine any possible outcome.

Australia's Angus Bell was yellow carded for a hip-drop tackle against England, but Prendergast's alleged offence was not penalised by match officials during the match.

If Prendergast receives a suspension, Connacht fly-half Ciaran Frawley would be the prime candidate to start against the Springboks on Saturday [16:40 GMT].

Ulster's Jamie Benson, who has yet to be capped at international level, is also an option for Farrell.

In better news for Ireland, captain Dan Sheehan is set to return for the game against the back-to-back world champions at the Aviva Stadium after he completed return to play protocols.

Sheehan - who is deputising for regular skipper Caelan Doris - missed Saturday's win over Fiji after sustaining a concussion in the defeat of Argentina on 6 November.

But in a squad update issued on Monday, the Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) said Sheehan will return to full training this week before the Springboks' visit to Dublin.

Ulster back row James McNabney is unavailable while he undergoes 12-day return to play protocols after sustaining a head injury that prematurely ended his eye-catching debut off the bench against the Fijians.

Tight-head prop Sam Illo is a doubt as he enters the return to play process, while utility back Jamie Osborne is ruled out with a pectoral injury that forced him off in the opening minutes of the Fiji game.

If Illo misses the Springboks game, Farrell has Thomas Clarkson and Tom O'Toole as back-up tight-head options with Tadhg Furlong expected to start.

Farrell will name his team to face the back-to-back world champions at 14:00 GMT on Thursday.

South Africa won last year's meeting 24-13 in Dublin but lost to France in Paris last weekend.

The harbour of Mytilene on the island of Lesbos in Greece. Thousands of refugees are arriving every day on Lesbos. Some of these will have opportunity to settle in Rwanda, or seek other alternatives with help from a safe home in Rwanda

For people who have spent years trying to build a future in Europe, being ordered to leave can mean returning to a country they may have left under difficult circumstances, or facing an uncertain future elsewhere.

A new arrangement involving Rwanda could offer another possibility: starting over in a different country.

Under a proposed partnership between Rwanda and five European countries, migrants transferred to Rwanda will have an opportunity to integrate into Rwandan society, with the option of voluntarily returning to their countries of origin or relocating to another country where they can legally settle.

The arrangement, announced on November 16, involves Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands. It targets people who are staying illegally in those countries and are subject to enforceable removal decisions.

But beyond the European effort to increase deportations, the arrangement introduces a different dimension to Rwanda’s migration policy: receiving people who may ultimately choose to make the country their home.

The distinction is important. Rather than simply serving as a transit point for people awaiting deportation, Rwanda is being positioned as a potential destination for migrants whose future in Europe has come to an end.

The joint announcement says those transferred will have an opportunity to integrate into Rwandan society.

International organisations will also support those who choose voluntary return or relocation to another country where they have legal permission to settle.

The practical arrangements, including the length of stay, integration support and the specific services available to migrants, are still being negotiated.

Rwanda has approached the arrangement as a partnership in which it retains the authority to determine who it accepts.

The proposed model does not mean that every person ordered to leave the five European countries will automatically be transferred to Rwanda. The receiving country will have a say in the selection process.

The European governments have also indicated that the pilot will exclude minors.

The Netherlands, for instance, has outlined an initial focus on adult men, although the selection criteria will differ among participating countries.

The arrangement will not apply to people who qualify for international protection or have another legal basis to remain in the five European countries.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the partnership reflects the country’s commitment to providing safe, legal and dignified solutions for migrants.

He also pointed to the global imbalance in economic opportunities as one of the factors driving irregular migration, arguing that international cooperation should address some of the conditions that push people into dangerous journeys.

The arrangement also has an economic dimension for Rwanda.

The five European countries will cover the costs associated with the programme, including the transfer and accommodation of migrants.

The wider partnership is also expected to create opportunities for cooperation in other areas of common interest.

The financial value of the arrangement, however, has not been disclosed.

For Rwanda, the potential benefits go beyond the resources committed to receiving and supporting migrants.

The initiative could also create opportunities in service provision and other areas associated with integration, although the scale of those opportunities will depend on the final agreement.

The six governments say they intend to develop the arrangement through a gradual process, with the first transfers targeted for 2027.

No official number of people to be transferred has been announced.

The involvement of international organisations will be an important part of the arrangement, particularly given the legal and human rights questions surrounding the transfer of migrants to countries outside Europe.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has provided technical input and is prepared, at Rwanda’s request, to provide care and assistance, subject to the necessary safeguards.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is also engaged in discussions, focusing on protecting asylum systems and ensuring that people who genuinely need international protection are not wrongly transferred.

The European Commission participated as an observer and contributed to discussions on implementation in line with European Union law.

The governments have committed to ensuring that the arrangement complies with Rwandan, European and international law, including human rights obligations.

The five European countries approached Rwanda to explore the possibility of establishing a migration return hub, according to details about the process.

Rwanda is retaining the sovereign right to determine which individuals it will accept under a selective screening process.

The migrants accepted will be received at designated facilities in Rwanda, including the Gashora centre in Bugesera District, which already has established infrastructure and capacity to accommodate migrants.

All logistical and operational costs associated with the arrangement will be covered by the participating European countries, while the partnership is also expected to generate economic benefits for Rwanda.

Upon arrival, the migrants will be granted legal migrant status in Rwanda, allowing them an opportunity to integrate into society. Those who wish to return to their countries of origin will be assisted and facilitated to do so.

Rwanda will work closely with relevant United Nations agencies and other international partners throughout the process to ensure that the arrangement meets international standards and provides the necessary protection and assistance.

The first group of migrants is expected to arrive in 2027, although no specific month or number has been announced.

However, important questions remain about how the safeguards will work in practice, the legal status of transferred migrants, their access to services and the mechanisms available to them if they challenge decisions affecting their rights.

For Rwanda, the initiative represents another significant engagement in international migration management.

Its ultimate success will depend not only on the number of people received but also on whether those arriving can build dignified and sustainable lives.

Ibihugu bitanu byo mu muryango w'Ubumwe bw'Uburayi (EU) byatangaje ko mu mwaka utaha bizafungura mu Rwanda ikigo cyo kwakira abimukira byirukanye, mu rwego rwa gahunda ngari yo kongera umubare w'abo byirukana.

Ubudage, Denmark, Autriche (Austria), Ubugereki n'Ubuholandi byitezwe gufungura "ikigo cy'abirukanwe" kizaba cyiteguye kubakira mu mwaka wa 2027, nkuko leta y'Ubuholandi na leta ya Denmark zabitangaje mu matangazo zasohoye.

Muri Kanama(8), u Rwanda na rwo rwatangaje ko rwatangiye ibiganiro by'ibanze n'ibihugu byinshi byo mu Burayi kuri uwo mushinga.

Biravugwa ko iyi gahunda izareba gusa abasabye ubuhungiro barangije kunyura mu nzira zose ziteganywa n'amategeko zabafashaga kuguma mu muryango w'Ubumwe bw'Uburayi, bitandukanye n'amasezerano yari yarasinywe n'Ubwongereza, ateganya kohereza mu Rwanda abantu kugira ngo abe ari ho babanza gusuzumirwa ubusabe bwabo bw'ubuhungiro.

Iyo gahunda y'Ubwongereza ntiyigeze ishyirwa mu bikorwa kubera ibibazo by'amategeko, nyuma iza gukurwaho na guverinoma y'ishyaka ry'abakozi (Labour), ryagiye ku butegetsi mu 2024.

Ibyo bihugu bitanu byo muri EU bivuga ko gahunda yo kohereza abimukira mu kindi gihugu ihuje n'amategeko y'uwo muryango ndetse n'amategeko mpuzamahanga. Icyakora, imiryango iharanira uburenganzira bwa muntu ivuga ko ishobora guhonyora uburenganzira bw'abimukira.

Aya masezerano aje nyuma y'ivugururwa riherutse gukorwa mu muryango w'Ubumwe bw'Uburayi, ryemereye ishyirwaho ry'ibigo nk'ibi hanze y'ibihugu biwugize.

Biteganyijwe ko ibisobanuro birambuye kuri uyu mushinga bizatangarizwa i Vienne ku wa Mbere. Amakuru aturuka mu nzego za dipolomasi yabwiye ibiro ntaramakuru AFP ko ikigo giteganyijwe mu Rwanda kizatangira nk'umushinga w'igerageza, kikazakira abantu bagera ku 100.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Buri gihugu muri ibyo bitanu gishobora koherezayo abimukira bagera kuri 20.

Ibi bihugu, bifite icyizere ko icyo kigo kizaba cyatangiye gukora mu mwaka wa 2027.

Umuryango Mpuzamahanga ushinzwe Abimukira (IOM) ushobora kugira uruhare mu gushyigikira uwo mushinga.

Umuvugizi wa IOM yagize ati: "IOM ifite amateka maremare yo gufasha abimukira bari mu rugendo, harimo no mu bihe bikomeye."

Yongeyeho ko uwo muryango urimo kuganira n'ibihugu bimwe byo muri EU ku bijyanye n'imishinga yo gushyiraho ibigo byakira abimukira basubizwa mu bihugu byabo cyangwa ubundi buryo busa na byo.

Mu gihe ibihugu byinshi byo muri EU byitegura amatora, za guverinoma zashyizweho igitutu cyo kwerekana ko zishoboye kugenzura ikibazo cy'abimukira.

Impungenge z'umutekano, ubukungu butifashe neza ndetse no kutanyurwa n'amashyaka ari ku butegetsi, biri mu byagize uruhare rukomeye mu buryo abaturage babona abava mu bihugu byabo bakajya gutura mu bindi.

Clementine de Montjoye, impuguke nkuru mu muryango Human Rights Watch, ikurikirana ibibera muri Afurika, yavuze ko guhitamo u Rwanda biteye impungenge, kuko icyo gihugu gifite "amateka azwi yo gucecekesha abatavuga rumwe na Leta, guta abantu muri yombi mu buryo bunyuranyije n'amategeko no kubafata nabi igihe bafunzwe", ndetse kikanashinjwa gufasha imitwe yitwaje intwaro ikorera muri Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo.

Yagize ati: "Guha Kigali amafaranga kugira ngo yakire gahunda yo kohereza abimukira basubizwa mu bihugu byabo ntibizateza imibabaro abo bantu bazaba boherejweyo gusa, ahubwo bizanagira uruhare mu gutera inkunga no guha imbaraga za politiki Leta ishinjwa guhonyora uburenganzira bwa muntu, haba imbere mu gihugu no hanze yacyo."

Ikigo cyigenga cya EU gishinzwe Uburenganzira bw'Ibanze bw'Abaturage na cyo cyavuze ko igihugu icyo ari cyo cyose cyakiriye ikigo nk'iki kigomba kubahiriza uburenganzira bw'ibanze bwa muntu, kuko abimukira batagomba koherezwa mu gihugu bashobora guhura n'ibibazo bikomeye by'itotezwa.

Iki kigo kandi cyavuze ko abana badafite ababyeyi cyangwa abandi babarera babaherekeje badakwiye koherezwa muri ibyo bigo.

Nk'uko byatangajwe n'Ikigo cy'Uburayi gishinzwe Kurinda Imipaka n'Inkombe z'Inyanja (Frontex), mu mezi 10 ya mbere ya 2026, abantu bagera ku 110.000 binjiye mu bihugu bigize EU mu buryo bunyuranyije n'amategeko.

Uyu mubare wagabanutseho 29% ugereranyije n'uwari wabonetse mu gihe nk'icyo cy'umwaka wabanje.

Mu kwezi k'Ukwakira(10) honyine, abantu bagera ku 18.100 binjiye muri ibyo bihugu mu buryo butemewe n'amategeko.

Uyu mubare wagabanutseho 6% ugereranyije n'abinjiye mu bihugu bigize EU mu kwezi kwa 10, umwaka wa 2025.

Ibi bikubiye mu itangazo ryashyizwe ahagaragara ku wa 16 Ugushyingo 2026, rivuga ko u Rwanda n'ibihugu birimo Austria, Denmark, u Budage, u Bugiriki n'u Buholandi biri gushakisha uburyo byashyiraho ikigo kizajya cyakira abimukira bavuye muri ibyo bihugu, kizwi nka Return Hub.

Iyi gahunda igamije gufasha ibihugu by'i Burayi gukemura ikibazo cy'abimukira binjira cyangwa baba ku butaka bwabyo mu buryo bunyuranyije n'amategeko, ariko ntibashobore gusubizwa mu bihugu bakomokamo nubwo baba barafatiwe ibyemezo byo kubasubiza iwabo.

Ibyo bihugu bivuga ko ubu buryo bushobora no guca intege abacuruza abantu, bakurura abimukira babizeza kubageza i Burayi, bakabashyira mu ngendo ziteje akaga.

Icyakora, gahunda iri kuganirwaho izareba gusa abimukira baba mu buryo bunyuranyije n'amategeko muri kimwe muri ibyo bihugu bitanu, kandi baramaze gufatirwa icyemezo gishobora gushyirwa mu bikorwa cyo kubasubiza iwabo cyangwa kubirukana. Ntizareba abantu bakeneye uburinzi mpuzamahanga cyangwa abafite izindi mpamvu zemewe n'amategeko zituma bemererwa kuguma muri ibyo bihugu.

Abazazanwa mu Rwanda bazahabwa amahirwe yo kuhatura no kwinjira mu buzima bw'Abanyarwanda, mu gihe abandi bazaba bemerewe guhitamo gusubira mu bihugu bakomokamo ku bushake cyangwa kujya mu kindi gihugu bemerewe guturamo mu buryo bwemewe n'amategeko.

Iryo tangazo rivuga ko imiryango mpuzamahanga n'u Rwanda bizagira uruhare mu kubafasha, haba mu kwinjira mu buzima bw'u Rwanda cyangwa mu gutegura urugendo rwo gusubira mu bihugu bakomokamo.

Minisitiri w'Ububanyi n'Amahanga n'Ubutwererane w'u Rwanda, Vincent Biruta, yavuze ko u Rwanda rwiyemeje gukorana n'ibihugu by'i Burayi mu gushakira abimukira ibisubizo byubahiriza amategeko, umutekano n'icyubahiro cya muntu.

Yagize ati: “U Rwanda ni igihugu cyakira impunzi n'abimukira, kandi twiyemeje gukorana n'abafatanyabikorwa bacu b'i Burayi kugira ngo dushakire abimukira ibisubizo bitekanye, byemewe n'amategeko kandi byubahiriza icyubahiro cyabo.”

Yakomeje avuga ko ubu bufatanye bushobora no gufasha gukemura ubusumbane bw'amahirwe mu bukungu ku isi, ari na kimwe mu bituma abantu, cyane cyane Abanyafurika, bafata ibyemezo byo kwimukira mu bindi bihugu mu buryo butemewe.

Minisitiri Biruta yongeyeho ko iyi gahunda ishobora kurokora ubuzima bw'abantu, kuko izafasha kurwanya amatsinda y'abagizi ba nabi yinjiza amafaranga mu gucuruza abantu no kubashora mu ngendo ziteje akaga.

Ku ruhande rw'ibihugu by'i Burayi, Minisitiri w'Umutekano wa Austria, Gerhard Karner, yavuze ko ibi biganiro ari intambwe ifatika mu gushyira mu bikorwa gahunda y'ibigo byakira abimukira hanze y'u Burayi.

Yavuze ko Austria, u Budage, Denmark, u Buholandi n'u Bugiriki byamaze kugira uruhare rukomeye mu guteza imbere ubu buryo, kandi ko ibiganiro bifatika n'u Rwanda bigiye gutangira.

Minisitiri wa Denmark, Morten Bødskov, we yavuze ko iyi gahunda ari intambwe ikomeye mu kuvugurura uburyo bwo gucunga ubuhunzi n'ubwimukira mu Muryango w'Ubumwe bw'u Burayi, kugira ngo abadafite uburenganzira bwo kuhatura bashobore gusubizwa ahandi.

Mu gihe u Budage buvuga ko ubu buryo bushobora gufasha abantu badafite uburenganzira bwo kuguma i Burayi kandi badafite icyizere cyo kuhaguma, u Bugiriki bwo buvuga ko buzafasha kugabanya ubwimukira butemewe no gusenya imiyoboro icuruza abantu.

U Buholandi na bwo buvuga ko gusubiza abantu badafite uburenganzira bwo kuguma mu gihugu ari ingenzi kugira ngo gahunda z'ubuhunzi zikore neza. Uruhare rw'imiryango mpuzamahanga Ibiganiro by'iyi gahunda birimo n'imiryango mpuzamahanga, irimo Komisiyo y'Ubumwe bw'u Burayi (European Commission), Ishami ry'Umuryango w'Abibumbye rishinzwe abimukira (IOM) n'Ishami ry'Umuryango w'Abibumbye ryita ku mpunzi (UNHCR).

Komisiyo y'Ubumwe bw'u Burayi iri gutanga ubujyanama ku buryo gahunda izashyirwa mu bikorwa hubahirizwa amategeko ya EU.

IOM na yo iri gutanga ubufasha mu bya tekiniki ku mikorere y'ikigo kizakira abimukira, ndetse ivuga ko yiteguye kugira uruhare mu kubitaho no kubafasha, mu gihe ingamba zikenewe zo kubarinda zaba zashyizweho.

UNHCR yo iri kuganira n'u Rwanda n'ibyo bihugu bitanu kugira ngo uburenganzira bw'abakeneye uburinzi mpuzamahanga bukomeze kubahirizwa, kandi isuzume niba gahunda izubahiriza amahame mpuzamahanga arengera uburenganzira bwa muntu.

U Rwanda ruvuga ko rwubahiriza amasezerano mpuzamahanga atandukanye arimo ajyanye n'uburenganzira bwa muntu, uburenganzira bw'impunzi, kurengera abakozi bimukira, gukumira iyicarubozo no kurengera abana.

U Rwanda n'ibyo bihugu bitanu byemeje ko ubu bufatanye buzashingira ku bwubahane n'inyungu z'impande zombi, kandi ko butazagarukira gusa ku bijyanye n'abimukira, ahubwo buzareba n'ibindi bibazo bihuriweho.

Biteganyijwe ko ibiganiro bizakomeza buhoro buhoro, hagamijwe kugera ku masezerano ashyiraho ubu buryo bwo kwakira abimukira, ku buryo ibikorwa byo kubohereza mu Rwanda byatangira mu 2027.

Icyakora, kugeza ubu ibyo bihugu biracyari mu biganiro byo kumvikana ku buryo nyabwo iyi gahunda izashyirwa mu bikorwa.

Amashyirahamwe y’umupira w’amaguru yo ku mugabane w'i Burayi ahagarariwe mu Nama Nyobozi ya UEFA no muri FIFA Council, yahurije ku gushyigikira Philippe Diallo, Perezida w’Ishyirahamwe ry’Umupira w’Amaguru mu Bufaransa (FFF), ku mwanya wa Perezida wa FIFA. Ibi byatangajwe kuri uyu wa Mbere, tariki ya 16 Ugushyingo 2026, nyuma y’inama yayobowe na Perezida wa UEFA, Aleksander Čeferin, aho ayo mashyirahamwe yasabye Diallo kwiyamamariza kuyobora FIFA mu matora ateganyijwe muri Werurwe 2027, anamwizeza inkunga yuzuye.

Philippe Diallo yemeye ubu busabe, ariko kandidatire ye irabanza kwemezwa ku mugaragaro n’Inama Nyobozi y'Ishyirahamwe ry'umupira w'amaguru mu Bufaransa (FFF) mu nama iteganyijwe kuri uyu wa Kabiri, tariki ya 17 Ugushyingo 2026.

Diallo afite ubunararibonye mu miyoborere y’umupira w’amaguru. Yigeze kuyobora urwego ruhagarariye amakipe y’umupira w’amaguru akina icyiciro cya mbere mu Bufaransa, aba mu Nama y’Ubutegetsi y’Urwego rw’Umupira w’Amaguru w'ababigize umwuga mu Bufaransa, anagira uruhare mu nzego za FIFA zishinzwe gukemura amakimbirane.

Mu 2023 ni bwo yabaye Perezida w’Ishyirahamwe ry’Umupira w’Amaguru mu Bufaransa (FFF) anaba umwe mu bagize Inama Nyobozi ya UEFA.

Mu itangazo ry'Amashyirahamwe y’umupira w’amaguru yo ku mugabane w'i Burayi, mu kumushyigikira bagaragaje ko FIFA ikeneye kongera kubaka ubumwe n’icyizere mu muryango w’umupira w’amaguru ku Isi, nyuma yo kugaragaza hari impungenge ku cyerekezo uyu muryango urimo.

Bashimangiye ko FIFA ikwiye gushyira imbere iterambere ry’umupira w’amaguru mu Turere twose tw’isi, gukorera mu mucyo no kubahiriza amahame akomeye y’imiyoborere myiza, ndetse no gukorana bya hafi n’amashyirahamwe ayigize, impuzamashyirahamwe n’abandi bafatanyabikorwa.

Ayo mashyirahamwe yavuze ko yizeye ko Philippe Diallo afite ubushobozi bwo gutanga umurongo w'ubuyobozi bukenewe kugira ngo izo ntego zigerweho.

Amatora ya Perezida wa FIFA ateganyijwe muri Werurwe 2027. Gushyigikirwa n’abahagarariye amashyirahamwe y’i Burayi ni intambwe ikomeye kuri Diallo, ariko kugira ngo atsinde nanone azakenera amajwi y’amashyirahamwe agize FIFA aturutse mu mpande zose z’isi.

Nicolas Jackson has 12 goals in 18 appearances for Aston Villa and Senegal this season

Nicolas Jackson was on target again as both Senegal and Cameroon moved to the brink of qualification for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with away victories.

After Aston Villa striker Jackson had opened the scoring, Senegal gave up a 2-0 lead against Sudan before two late goals sealed a 4-2 win, while five-time Afcon winners Cameroon cruised to a 3-0 triumph over Namibia.

Both sides are on 10 points in their respective groups after four rounds of matches and will progress to next year's finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda if other results go their way on Tuesday.

Elsewhere, Jordan Ayew's first-half penalty was enough for Ghana to register back-to-back victories over Somalia in Group C.

The Black Stars had home advantage for what should have been an away tie, with the game played in Sekondi-Takoradi because the Ocean Stars do not have a stadium fit for international football.

Ayew had a penalty saved as Ghana beat Somalia 2-0 in the reverse fixture last Thursday, but the Sheffield United forward kept his composure when he sent the goalkeeper the wrong way in the 36th minute after Brandon Thomas-Asante had been pulled down in the box.

Ghana, who parted company with Carlos Queiroz after losing their opening two fixtures, move level in the table with The Gambia, with both sides on six points.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

The Gambians are themselves three points adrift of group leaders Ivory Coast before they host the Elephants on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Zimbabwe beat Equatorial Guinea 3-0 in Harare to go two points behind Group E table toppers DR Congo.

Thando Ngwenya, Tawanda Chirewa and Tawanda Maswanhise were all on target for the Warriors before Equatorial Guinea's Josete Miranda had a penalty saved and Saul Coco was sent off for the visitors late on.

The National Thunder were without first choice goalkeeper Jesus Owono after he asked not to be selected following his involvement in a collision with Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the day after the incident.

DR Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali and Morocco can all book their tickets to the tournament when the fourth round of fixtures culminates with 18 matches on Tuesday.

The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in East Africa from 19 June to 17 July.

Patrick Vieira's Senegal survived a scare in neutral Juba after Jackson's early goal put the Teranga Lions ahead and a low strike from Brentford left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf made it 2-0 midway through the first half.

Sudan hit back through Al-Gozoli Nooh and Salah Adel to level proceedings with 15 minutes to play, but Pathe Mboup's lob made it 3-2 in the 87th minute and Paul Mendy made the points safe for the West Africans in the first minute of added time.

Senegal are still awaiting the outcome of their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport over the destination of the 2025 Afcon title.

The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in January's final, but a Confederation of African Football appeals board stripped them of the title two months later, decreeing Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.

Mahamadou Nagida opened the scoring for Cameroon against Namibia in neutral Botswana with a stunning volley from outside the box in the 12th minute, and Ryan Fosso's deflected effort doubled the lead just before the hour mark.

Saidou Alioum made it 3-0 with a fine first-time volley with 19 minutes remaining, and David Pagou's men will be assured of a place at Afcon 2027 if Congo-Brazzaville fail to beat Comoros on Tuesday.

Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.

Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.

"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."

She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."

Posting on Instagram , external , she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.

"Watch this space and look ready. I am… More soon."

Watch: Forensic expert Michael Freeman speaks to Newsnight about Epstein's death

This article contains distressing details and references to suicide

A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.

Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.

Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.

He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings at University College London on Monday evening.

Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.

Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein.

He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.

Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.

He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".

He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."

The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , external that Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.

Epstein was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges when he was found dead in his cell

Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.

According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.

Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.

When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".

"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.

Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."

"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."

"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.

Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.

Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

Watch: Date announced for Lindsay Clancy retrial

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.

The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.

Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.

Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.

Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.

Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.

Clancy with her ex-husband and their children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan

The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.

A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.

Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.

The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.

Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.

It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.

The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.

The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.

Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces

For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.

In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.

Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.

On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.

Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.

But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.

Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.

The ministry has defended , external Agnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.

But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.

Those selected are trained for months before being inducted into regiments

When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.

But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.

"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.

These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.

The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.

This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.

Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.

The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.

"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.

The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported , external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.

Many young men from small towns spend months preparing for the selection process to join the defence forces

But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.

Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued , external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.

Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.

"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.

"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."

Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.

Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI , external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.

But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.

Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.

Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.

Indian soldiers are deployed through the year at the country's borders with China and Pakistan

There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget , external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.

By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.

"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.

He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.

Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.

"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.

Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.

"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."

The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.

The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.

For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.

But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

The announcement was made on Monday on the official 007 social media accounts

Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

Hollywood reacts to Robert Pattinson being cast as new James Bond

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply gratreful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

'Big shoes to fill': Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Robert Pattinson has starred in Twilight, Tenet, The Batman and The Odyssey

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".

"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."

At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.

Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, , external rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.

Pattinson shot to fame in Harry Potter and went on to star in Twilight opposite Kristen Stewart (pictured in 2011)

Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire,

He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.

Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.

He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.

But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Daniel Craig was a popular 007 and appeared in five James Bond films

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

The Rwanda Development Board (RDB) is exploring opportunities to strengthen the country’s connections with international investors and promote sustainable business growth through improved family business governance and long-term wealth management.

RDB Chief Executive Officer Jean-Guy Afrika held discussions with Barry Johnson, Founder and President of the 7 Generations Institute, an organisation that supports business-owning families in managing their enterprises and preserving wealth across generations.

The discussions focused on family business governance, sustainable wealth management and opportunities to connect Rwanda more closely with international investor networks to encourage long-term investment in the country.

A key area of interest was how family-owned enterprises can establish strong governance structures, improve succession planning and adopt sustainable management practices to ensure their businesses remain competitive and continue creating value for future generations.

Johnson’s experience in advising business-owning families offers opportunities for Rwanda to explore approaches that strengthen locally owned enterprises while encouraging more international investment partnerships.

The engagement also highlighted the importance of building connections between Rwandan businesses and global networks of investors, particularly those interested in long-term investment opportunities and sustainable wealth creation.

By promoting sound corporate governance, responsible wealth management and international business linkages, Rwanda aims to create a stronger investment environment, support the growth of family-owned enterprises and encourage investments that deliver lasting economic benefits.

The discussions reflect Rwanda’s broader ambition to attract sustainable capital, strengthen private-sector capacity and position the country as an attractive destination for investors seeking long-term opportunities.

By engaging investors directly, Rwanda is seeking to position itself as an attractive destination for mining investment while creating opportunities for knowledge transfer, technology adoption and stronger private-sector cooperation.

Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"

The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices -having previously welcomed it.

Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.

She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.

A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".

Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.

"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.

She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

What happens next in Yemen may send fresh shockwaves to the world economy

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.

Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.

Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.

The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.

Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.

But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.

Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?

When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.

The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.

But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.

On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.

Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."

He warns that if the port of Aden – a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants – was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".

But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.

"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."

"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."

It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.

The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.

He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.

"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.

"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

Sir Tom Jones cancelled or rescheduled four dates on the US-leg of his tour last month due to illness

Sir Tom Jones has announced two headline shows in Wales just weeks after he was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of tour dates due to illness.

The 86-year-old Welsh music icon's homecoming, as part of his Come Gather Round world tour, will see him perform at Cardiff Castle on 30 May, followed by a fully-seated show at Llangollen Pavilion in Denbighshire on 28 June.

Heather Small will feature as a special guest at the Cardiff show, while soul band Stone Foundation will also join the bill at both concerts.

It is a return to home soil for the legendary singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, who last performed in Wales in summer 2025.

Last month, Sir Tom was forced to cancel or reschedule shows in the US-leg of the world tour, due to "a bad case of flu".

He said at the time that he was "truly sorry" for the disappointment caused to fans, later adding he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital.

Tickets for his Welsh gigs go on sale on 20 November, and the sets will feature tracks from his 2021 album Surrounded By Time, alongside fan favourites including It's Not Unusual, What's New Pussycat?, Delilah and Green, Green Grass of Home.

Nick Saunders, founder of promoter Depot Live, said: "Tom Jones is a true Welsh icon, so it's a real pleasure to welcome him back to Cardiff Castle.

"He's one of Wales' greatest-ever musical exports, and there's always a real sense of pride in seeing him perform on home soil."

Dave Danford, artistic director of the Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod, added: "His show here in 2024 was one of the most memorable evenings in the venue's history, and we've been trying to find a way to get him back here ever since."

Louise, 30, says her addiction to decongestants left her feeling like a prisoner in her own body

A woman says her blocked nose left her with a decade-long addiction to decongestant nasal sprays that cost her thousands.

Louise Gough, 30, failed to read the fine print on her over-the-counter Sudafed which warns it is for short-term use only, and ended up addicted.

She came so reliant on the medication she was spraying up to 15 times a day and felt like a "prisoner in her own body".

Sudafed said the safe use of its products was its top priority.

But a consultant surgeon who treats this dependency said the warning should be more prominent on packaging.

Gough, from Caerphilly, estimates she spent about £2,000, secretly buying bottles that cost about £7 because her partner was frustrated by her spending.

"I used it [when I had a cold] and instantly within 10 seconds my nose was unblocked," she said.

"It's partly my fault. I didn't read the box and I didn't realise that you could only use it for a certain amount in a time period.

"No one ever warned me when I bought it. It just turned into a really vicious cycle."

Prolonged use can make congestion worse, so even when Gough did not have a cold, her nose would be blocked and she would use the spray.

She had developed rhinitis medicamentosa, a medication-induced nasal congestion also known as rebound congestion.

"I found myself feeling really anxious if I didn't have a bottle on me," she said.

"This was particularly bad if I was out with my partner as I'd ask him to get me one and he'd be annoyed.

"I laugh about it now but it wasn't funny at the time.

"I felt like a prisoner in my own body and I couldn't get away from it."

Louise says she felt anxious when she did not have a nasal spray with her

Ear, nose and throat (ENT) consultant Vik Veer said decongestant sprays work by temporarily restricting blood flow to the nasal lining.

Prolonged use can trigger a cycle in which the nose becomes increasingly congested as the medication wears off.

"The thing you were doing to try to make you better actually makes you even worse," he said.

"Every ENT surgeon will know about [rebound congestion] and would see this problem almost in every clinic."

Official recommendations are that nasal decongestant sprays , external containing xylometazoline and oxymetazoline should not be used for more than five consecutive days.

But Veer said he believes rebound congestion can begin much sooner.

"I think the evidence points towards you having problems within three days of using these sprays," he said.

When Gough started taking decongestants, the recommendation was seven days, with the current five-day warning added to packaging in 2026.

When Gough used two bottles in 11 days on her family holiday to Greece she said she knew she had to quit, and stopped taking them three years ago.

"It's like someone has shoved something so far up your nose you physically can't breathe at all," she said.

The first few days off the medication made her feel "claustrophobic in her own body" as she struggled to breathe naturally, she said. But after a month she was finally able to breathe through her nose unmedicated.

But Gough has not regained her sense of taste and smell as strongly as before.

A Sudafed spokesperson said its products followed strict regulatory and industry rules, with usage information provided on packaging, patient information leaflets and its website.

It encouraged anyone with questions about using its products to speak to a GP or pharmacist.

Angry captain Andy Robertson says Scotland do not have time to turn things around after a brutal 4-0 defeat by Switzerland consigned them to a third-place finish in their Nations League group.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli - appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August - has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.

They collapsed worryingly easily in St Gallen against a much-changed Swiss outfit on Monday after a promising start, Bologna midfielder Lewis Ferguson putting through his own goal and early intensity gave way to indecision.

The Swiss struck twice in the early minutes of the second half to make it 3-0 and Zeki Amdouni made it four late on.

'You do not have time in international football'

"First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player.

"By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football.

"It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it.

"These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."
